title: Opus5.5 Low to Max - Now in Three.JS ( you guys asked for this)
author: 314t
selftext:
you guys asked for this

We did low to max in godot. 

We did low to max in unreal. 

Now we have low to max in three.js.

What should we do next?

|Model|Effort|Tokens in (incl. cache)|Cached|Tokens out|Time|Cost|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
||
|Opus 5.5|low|8.07M|98%|54k|17m 28s|$3.86|
|Opus 5.5|medium|22.79M|99%|112k|42m 18s|$8.72|
|Opus 5.5|high|16.70M|98%|93k|21m 29s|$7.17|
|Opus 5.5|xhigh|38.64M|99%|228k|38m 20s|$15.82|
|Opus 5.5|max|81.90M|99%|513k|1h 22m 17s|$34.35|

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body: Thanks for listening to my request and it's really surprising how well it turned out, wow! I did not expect three.js to be able to be this pretty.

comments.author: owen800q
comments.body: seem max output is best otherwise high

comments.author: Longjumping-Tough581
comments.body: I feel like Max made a real difference compared to the others. I also don't understand why Medium effort spent more tokens than High?

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Honestly for most purposes low is fine, spending 10x to double the result is not efficient for a solo dev.

Can also run the whole project on low, then high for the final polish.

comments.author: TheBigQuestion354
comments.body: In my experience Max is easily the best. I know it’s token hungry but despite what others may say it definitely works. Fixed a problem in 20 minutes the other day that extra worked for 4 hours on and couldn’t solve.
